title: UPSC CSE - Ancient India - Gupta and Post-Gupta Age
subject: Ancient India

questions.q: Sanghabhuti, an Indian Buddhist monk, who travelled to China at the end of the fourth century AD, was the author of a commentary on:
questions.explain: The complete Sarvāstivāda Vinaya is extant in the Chinese Buddhist canon. In its early history, the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya was the most common vinaya tradition in China. Sanghabhuti is the author of a commentary on the Sarvastivada Vinaya.

questions.q:
With reference to the history of ancient India, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. Mitakshara was the civil law for upper castes and Dayabhaga was the civil law for lower castes.
2. In the Mitakshara system, the sons can claim right to the property during the lifetime of the father, whereas in the Dayabhaga system, it is only after the death of the father that the sons can claim right to the property.
3. The Mitakshara system deals with the matters related to the property held by male members only of a family, whereas the Dayabhaga system deals with the matters related to the property held by both male and female members of a family.
questions.explain: Statement 1 is incorrect as Mitakshara and Dayabhaga are not based on caste divisions. Statement 2 is correct regarding the difference in property rights between the two systems. Statement 3 is incorrect as both systems deal with property held by male and female members, though Dayabhaga gives more rights to women.

questions.q:
From the decline of Guptas until the rise of Harshavardhana in the early seventh century, which of the following kingdoms were holding power in Northern India?
1. The Guptas of Magadha
2. The Paramaras of Malwa
3. The Pushyabhutis of Thanesar
4. The Maukharis of Kanauj
5. The Yadavas of Devagiri
6. The Maitrakas of Valabhi
questions.explain: The Later Guptas of Magadha, the Pushyabhutis of Thanesar, the Maukharis of Kanauj, and the Maitrakas of Valabhi were holding power in Northern India during the mentioned period. The Paramaras and Yadavas belonged to later periods.

questions.q: Which of the following phrases defines the nature of the 'Hundi' generally referred to in the sources of the post-Harsha period?
options: An advisory issued by the king to his subordinates
A diary to be maintained for daily accounts
An order from the feudal lord to his subordinates
questions.explain: Hundi was an instrument of credit or a bill of exchange used during the Medieval period to facilitate the transfer of money from one part of the country to another. It was a letter of credit payable after a period at a discount.

questions.q: With reference to the period of the Gupta dynasty in ancient India, the towns Ghantasala, Kadura, and Chaul were known as
options: places of exquisite stone art and architecture
questions.explain: During the Gupta period, Ghantasala, Kadura, and Chaul were known as ports handling foreign trade. These ports were part of the extensive maritime trade network between India, Southeast Asia, and China.

questions.q: With reference to the history of India, the terms 'kulyavapa' and 'dronavapa' denote
questions.explain: In the Gupta period, 'kulyavapa' and 'dronavapa' were terms used for the measurement of land. These were different land measures known in different regions, along with other terms like Nivartana.

questions.q:
With reference to the scholars/litterateurs of ancient India, consider the following statements:
1. Panini is associated with Pushyamitra Shunga
2. Amarasimha is associated with Harshavardhana
3. Kalidasa is associated with Chandra Gupta-II
questions.explain: Panini lived during the Mahajanapada era, not during Pushyamitra Shunga's time. Amarasimha was associated with the Gupta dynasty, not Harshavardhana. Kalidasa was indeed associated with Chandra Gupta-II (also known as Vikramaditya).
questions.subject: Ancient India

questions.q: With reference to forced labour (Vishti) in India during the Gupta period, which one of the following statements is correct?
options: It was considered a source of income for the State, a sort of tax paid by the people.
It was totally absent in the Madhya Pradesh and Kathiawar regions of the Gupta Empire.
The forced labourer was entitled to weekly wages.
The eldest son of the labourer was sent as the forced labourer.
questions.explain: During the Gupta period, Vishti (forced labour) was considered a source of income for the State, a sort of tax paid by the people. It is mentioned in Gupta era copper inscriptions as one form of tax, suggesting it was extracted from regions like Gujarat and Malwa.

questions.q:
The Chinese traveller Yuan Chwang (Hiuen Tsang) who visited India recorded the general conditions and culture of India at that time. In this context, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. The roads and river routes were completely immune from robbery.
2. As regards punishment for offences, ordeals by fire, water, and poison were the instruments for determining the innocence or guilt of a person.
3. The tradesmen had to pay duties at ferries and barrier stations.
questions.explain: According to Yuan Chwang's records, the roads and river routes were not completely immune from robbery. He described that travelling was not very safe at that time. The ordeals by fire, water, and poison were indeed used to determine innocence or guilt. Tradesmen had to pay light duties at ferries and barrier stations.

questions.q: India maintained its early cultural contacts and trade links with Southeast Asia across the Bay of Bengal. For this pre-eminence of early maritime history of Bay of Bengal, which of the following could be the most convincing explanation/explanations?
options: As compared to other countries, India had better ship-building technology in ancient and medieval times.
The rulers of southern India always patronised traders, brahmin priests and Buddhist monks in this context.
Monsoon winds across the Bay of Bengal facilitated sea voyages.
Both (a) and (b) are convincing explanations in this context.
questions.explain: India had advanced ship-building technology since ancient times, as evidenced by texts like Yuktikalpataru. The rulers of southern India patronized traders, Brahmin priests, and Buddhist monks, which facilitated cultural and trade contacts. While monsoon winds did facilitate sea voyages, this was not the main reason for India's pre-eminence in early maritime history of the Bay of Bengal.
